### EPITHALAMION.

O Christ, the <term>Logos</term> <gloss>Word</gloss> coming, who fell from the ether of the Father,
You enter the chaste womb of an untouched Virgin.
You are born into the world, promised to the fathers before,
You repair what perished through the serpent's wiles.
You destroy the devastating realms of horrific Satan,
You return thence as an everlasting Victor and Standard-bearer.
You carry with You the gifts which Your Victory produced,
These true blessings are birthed by Your blood.
You who send the paternal <term>Pneuma</term> <gloss>Spirit</gloss> into human minds,
So that hearts may truly please God.
Come here, Prince, to the holy Altar, while she is being led,
She who is to be the illustrious Spouse to the illustrious Duke.
With You as Leader, suggest the celestial breath from the Father's breast,
Which may join the two in chaste love.
Because the Hero has known You here from his tender years,
And has concern for pure religion.
Because this young woman has revered You with modest prayers,
And honors You with sincere piety.
And because You promise: "Whoever loves me alone,
And joyfully carries my words in his heart,
I shall meet him, and with the sacred Spirit,
We three wish to inhabit that house."
Then, because You approved of Marriage according to the custom of the fathers,
You also teach that You are its author.
Indeed, You were led to the Hymenæal joys,
And the cohort beloved with Your mother.

### Records of Things Heard, Volume 3: Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate

○ Even if a thing or affair is large, it is "below form" <gloss>physical</gloss>. Even if a <term>Principle</term> is small, it is "above form" <gloss>metaphysical</gloss>. <term>Principle</term> cannot truly be described as large or small. Here, calling <term>Principle</term> "small" is only to contrast the <term>Principle</term> found in a single small object with a very large thing, such as Heaven and Earth. It is like saying: "Heaven and Earth are indeed large, but they are 'below form.' The <term>Principle</term> of a single thing is indeed small, but it is 'above form'." This also must be looked at with flexibility. ○ Master <term>Huang Mianzai</term> asked: "The <term>Supreme Ultimate</term> cannot move or be still by itself. Since these are already <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>, how can we say it 'produces' <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>?" The answer was: "Producing <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term> is like <term>Yang</term> producing <term>Yin</term>," and so on. Since <term>Confucius</term> said the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term> produces the <term>Two Modes</term>, and Master <term>Zhou</term> said the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term> produces <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>, the Sages and Worthies clearly did not mind saying that <term>Principle</term> produces <term>Energy</term>. Today, why do some people hate this theory and avoid saying it, insisting instead that <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term> produce themselves without originating from the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term>? What is their intention? 

<column-break/>

The statement "We see the movement of the millstone because of the movement of the ant" <note>an analogy where the millstone is the universe and the ant is the Supreme Ultimate</note> is also an "inverted" way of speaking. It is correct to say: "Because of the movement and stillness of <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>, we can see the movement and stillness of the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term>." But it is incorrect to say: "Because of the movement and stillness of the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term>, we see the movement and stillness of <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>." Perhaps the two characters for "mill" and "ant" were swapped by mistake. Also, looking at the context, after the phrase "cannot move or be still by itself," there should be more words about "movement and stillness" that have been lost. ○ One must look at the word "observe" <gloss>guan</gloss>. It means I go inside the thing to take it apart and look at it. It does not mean the thing itself has "two faces." <term>Principle</term> and <term>Energy</term> are definitely two separate things, but they cannot be separated. This is <term>Master Zhu</term>'s teaching. One is hidden and one is manifest; they are clearly "two faces." But if the thing itself did not originally have two faces, how could I "take it apart" to look at it? ○ "Benefit and Firmness <gloss>Li-zhen</gloss> are <term>Nature</term> and <term>Emotion</term> <gloss>Xing-qing</gloss>." "When movement reaches its limit, there is stillness; when stillness reaches its limit, there is movement again." After "Nature and Emotion," there should be the sentence: "This is the stillness of the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term>." Otherwise, the text does not make sense. This matches the context. ○ Master <term>Cai Jiezhai</term> said: "Form <gloss>xing</gloss> means it moves and can be seen..."

# HISTORY OF THE HEBREW CHURCH. Chapter V.

<margin>
* See also our marginal commentators on Joshua 13:3.
</margin>

<margin>
The Nile and Sichor both named for their black color.
</margin>

<margin>
And how this river on the side of Egypt or the Southwest forms the boundaries of Canaan. And why it is slightly changed in our small map. *
</margin>

...to determine the boundaries; but also even from the name of the river *Sichor*: for just as *Sichor* <note>original Hebrew: שִׁיחוֹר (Shihor), meaning black or dark</note> means "blackish," it is generally testified that the Nile stream has blackish water; so that it is the same as if one said, *The Black River*: just as here with us, it is still called the *Swarte Water* <note>The Zwarte Water (Black Water) is a river in the Netherlands; the author uses this local comparison to help his Dutch readers understand the naming convention.</note>. Likewise the Greeks, according to Plutarchus and Eustathius, also called this river *Melas* <note>Greek: Μέλας, meaning black.</note>, and the Latins *Melo*, after its black color. Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a renowned Dutch scholar of history and chronology.</note> also derived the word *Sirin*, with which the Ethiopians name the Nile, from the Hebrew word *Sichor*; as has been noted elsewhere in the *Jewish Antiquities*. In such a way that one must at least likely conclude that *Nahal* <note>Hebrew for "brook" or "valley river."</note> and *Sichor* here do not mean the Nile any further than that we should understand by them merely an arm of that great river which flows out at Rhinokorrura <note>A coastal town between Egypt and Palestine, modern-day El Arish.</note>. Thus all the maps in the magnificent atlases and the Bible maps are deficient in this regard and need to be corrected. For although most are not negligent in making this river a boundary of Judea, they nevertheless show it so wide and emerging entirely on its own that no one could ever have considered it an arm of the Nile. Perhaps Strabo <note>A Greek geographer from the 1st century BCE/CE.</note> indicated it better, who, above the great Pelusian mouth of the Nile, places a smaller river by Mount Casius; to which he, along with many other writers, extends the boundary of Judea. Being, however, not so very far from Rhinokorrura, which city was so named after the truncated noses of its citizens <note>The name Rhinokorrura comes from the Greek for "cut-off noses," referring to a legend that the city was a penal colony for criminals whose noses had been mutilated.</note>. Therefore, it should seem strange to no one that a small change is perceived in our map in this vicinity. And although this river is so small that it only deserves the name of a *brook* and was not even navigable by any vessels, it should not surprise us when Holy Scripture calls it the *River of Egypt* and *Sichor*, as if it intended to signify the great bosom of the Nile itself thereby; since it is very common that in things of the same kind, especially water, the name of the whole is also given to its part. As for what further concerns the Nile stream itself, we shall speak more extensively of that in another place.

<margin>
Boundaries of Canaan indicated to the North and Northeast.
</margin>

<margin>
Whether Abraham's descendants ever possessed the Land of Canaan in the extent promised, namely from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates or the Great River.
</margin>

If we have then correctly found the divine boundary of Canaan to the South or Southwest against Egypt, we have no more difficulty remaining in discovering the same to the North or Northeast at the Euphrates, which Moses, not unjustly, calls *The Great River*. As to which our map sufficiently indicates the situation of its course; already described enough by us previously. But there another dispute arises to be brought from black darkness into the light: namely, how and where one shall correctly place the fulfillment of the promise in this wide region of the land? Since not only did the Jews never have all the provinces situated between these two rivers—the Nile and the Euphrates—in hereditary possession (which is nevertheless promised in plain words); but also, in Numbers 34, the possession of the land is not given to Israel further than *Hamath*, which is truly still very far on this side of the Euphrates. But let us hear the opinions of the scholars and then choose which one we wish to support. Jerome <note>original: Hieronymus, the 4th-century Church Father who translated the Vulgate.</note>, and after him Masius <note>Andreas Masius (1514–1573), a Flemish priest and humanist scholar of the Near East.</note> with others, are of the opinion that the promise of such a broad possession of the land was made under the condition of a laudable obedience on the part of Abraham's seed, that is *Israel*: which not having been proven by them later, God was released from His word of promise and was not bound to fulfill it to the end. To which one might remark that if the promise was made under condition, such an implicit condition must then rather apply to the whole promise and not only to certain parts of it...

<margin>25</margin> The querent's village is like his own body; some things are held in the mind. From there, one should judge the work to be done. From the <term>Ascendant</term> <note>original: "Lagna"; the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon</note>, if a planet is in the third house <note>original: "Sahaja"; literally 'born together', referring to siblings</note>, one speaks of siblings. If in the fifth house, one speaks of a son or grandson. If in the fourth house, one should speak of the mother or the mother's sister <note>maternal aunt</note>. If in the sixth house, one speaks of a foe or enemy. If in the seventh house, one speaks of the wife <note>original: "Jaya"</note>, especially based on the strength of the planets residing in the seventh from the Ascendant. If in the ninth house, which is the house of <term>Dharma</term> <note>religion, duty, or the father</note>, one should speak of matters related to merit and religion. In the tenth house, one speaks of the teacher <note>original: "Guru"</note>, masters, and horses.

The lord of the <term>Navamsha</term> <note>the ruler of the specific 1/9th division of the sign</note> occupied by the Lord of the Ascendant at that time determines the desire of the querent. If that lord is auspicious and well-placed, the outcome is good. If the lord of the house of enemies is situated in the Ascendant at the time of the query, then one should speak of an enemy. Now, regarding the placement of "faults" or "strengths" in the houses: among the many planets, the one that is most powerful determines the location or state of the querent’s desire. <margin>Rama</margin> Furthermore, in the same manner, by looking at the planetary strengths, one can determine if a person is surrounded by friends or if the rest are enemies, as shown in the books of <term>Jataka</term> <note>natal astrology</note>. <margin>25</margin>

Now, the knowledge regarding the "Thoughts on Travel" <note>original: "Pravasa Chinta"</note> is stated:

**Regarding the Movable Signs... || 51 ||**
When the <term>Movable Navamshas</term> <note>Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn</note> are rising in the seventh house or the Ascendant at the time of the query, one should speak of travel.

---

One should speak of the querent's travel from the <term>Navamshaka</term>. If the lord of the Ascendant is in a certain position, the person is thinking of journeying to a foreign land. Here is the specific certainty: regarding the seventh and ninth houses. From the Ascendant, if there is a planet in the seventh house that is <term>Retrograde</term> <note>original: "Vakrita"; appearing to move backward in the sky</note>, then the traveler who has gone abroad will return. If the planet is not retrograde, or if the sign in the seventh or ninth house is not occupied by a returning planet, then the person will not return.

Now, if the querent asks: "What kind of woman will I have a connection with?" that knowledge is provided:

**The Sun and others... || 52 ||**
Based on whether the Sun, Venus <note>original: "Sita"</note>, Mars <note>original: "Vakra"</note>, or Mercury <note>original: "Saumya"</note> are in the seventh house <note>the house of partnerships</note>, one predicts the woman. If the Sun is there, it may be another's wife. If Jupiter <note>original: "Jiva"</note> is there, one should say the woman is a lawful wife. If Mercury is present, she may be a woman of the merchant class <note>original: "Vaishya"</note> or a supporter. If the Moon is there, she is a courtesan. Similarly, if Saturn <note>original: "Sora" or "Shanishchara"</note> is in the seventh house, one should say he approaches a woman from an outcaste or very ignorant family.

The age and status of these women are known from the Moon: if the Moon is in its early phase, she is a young girl; if in its middle phase, she is a youthful woman; if in its late phase, she is an elderly woman. These have been shown by the wise in previous teachings. Now, the signs of illness and the knowledge of recovery will be spoken of.

At that time, when one holds that one should act only upon the words of one who is free from faults, if one maintains that action should only follow a thorough examination of the person, there will only be inaction and never any engagement. Why is that? It is because one cannot directly recognize a person who possesses qualities such as seeing the truth of reality as it is. This objection points out that action would never occur; it does not mean that persons endowed with qualities such as seeing the truth of reality as it is are undesirable. We certainly hold that such individuals exist, and they speak the truth. Why is that? It is because such persons who possess qualities like seeing reality as it is teach without error, presenting things precisely as they are.

Why then is it impossible to know such a person? The text states, <term>pramāṇa</term> <gloss>means of valid cognition</gloss>, and so forth. Whether this person possesses faults or does not possess faults, but rather is entirely faultless, this is the context. When it is said that even if another is faultless, it is difficult to know, this expression of being difficult to comprehend is presented in the feminine singular with reference to the faultlessness of another. Then, regarding the faults of another, the phrase "difficult to know" is inflected and connected in the masculine plural. Why is that? Because the <term>pramāṇa</term> <gloss>means of valid cognition</gloss> that ascertain the qualities and faults of another person are rare and hard to acquire.

The text explains this with the words "persons" and so on. Those persons who exhibit the characteristics of bodily and verbal actions that engage either correctly or erroneously are those who engage properly or improperly. Mental factors are mental occurrences, namely qualities and faults. nit ? Solutio. Ars musicæ similitudo soni & vocis de arbore elementali egressa, in qua se habet primo secundū naturam ad sua accidentia quam ad accidentia, aliarum arborum. Musicus in qua litera vocali primo incipit ad considerandum artem musicæ? Solutio. Nullus accentus ita communis est, nec ita leuis, sicut accentus de a. ### *De Quæstionibus Astronomiæ.*

PRincipia Astronomiæ quæ sunt ? Solutio. Vade ad rubricam antedictam. Astronomus considerat ante in sole habitum caloris quam lucis? Solutio. Nullus habitus appropriatus est ita considerabilis sicut habitus proprius. Astronomus quomodo facit iudicium? Solutio. Astronomus considerat respectum, quem vnum signū habet cum alio, & quem habet cum vna planeta per respectum lineæ diametricæ, & facit iudicium de hominibus qui nascuntur in illa linea, aut qui in illa faciunt, petitiones quos iudicat secundum conditiones signi & planetæ. Et valde ad rubricam virtutis. Quare scientia astronomiæ magis incerta est quam alia ? Solutio. de nulla scientia est ita grauis experientia sicut de astronomia, nec aliqua scientia est ita positiua sicut illa.
